opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think "coverage" is one of those words that gets used in a few different ways, so let me separate them.

The first, and I'd say the most neglected, is coverage of the population you actually care about. When we evaluate a model, we usually report a single aggregate number, like accuracy or AUC on a held-out test set. That number is an average, and averages can hide a lot. A model can look excellent overall while performing quite badly on particular subgroups, whether defined by demographics, geography, or some combination of features nobody thought to check. Much of my work on algorithmic fairness came from taking that seriously. If you only look at a handful of predefined groups, like race or gender, you can satisfy fairness constraints on each of them individually and still be badly wrong on their intersections. That's the "fairness gerrymandering" problem. So one notion of coverage I care about is: have you evaluated the model over a rich enough collection of subgroups that you'd actually notice if it were failing someone?

The second notion is more statistical: coverage in the sense of uncertainty quantification. If your model produces a prediction interval or a prediction set, does it contain the true answer at the rate it claims? That's where conformal prediction has been really valuable, because it gives you distribution-free guarantees. But the standard guarantee is marginal. It holds on average over the whole population, which brings us right back to the first issue. You can get 90% coverage overall while getting 70% on one group and 99% on another. So some of the more interesting recent work, which some of my colleagues and I have been involved in, asks for coverage guarantees that hold conditionally across many overlapping groups at once, sometimes called multivalid or multicalibrated coverage.

The third notion is coverage of the input space, or of deployment conditions. Your test set is a sample from some distribution, and the world you deploy into is almost never exactly that distribution. So you have to ask whether your evaluation covers the situations the model will really face, including rare or adversarial ones. For large generative models in particular, the space of possible inputs is so vast that any benchmark is a tiny sliver of it, and I think people sometimes overinterpret benchmark scores for that reason.

The unifying theme is that a single number rarely tells you what you need to know. The right way to think about evaluation is to specify up front the many ways you could be wrong, and the many populations or conditions you care about, and then design your evaluation, and ideally your training, to give you guarantees across all of them simultaneously. The nice thing is that there's now a fairly well-developed algorithmic toolkit for doing exactly that, often with surprisingly modest statistical cost. So it's not just a philosophical aspiration anymore. It's something practitioners can really implement.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes coverage of prediction sets or intervals (whether they contain the true answer) from coverage of the input space and deployment conditions.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss face recognition or say that its input coverage should include natural variation in facial images.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: So when I talk about coverage, I'm really thinking about something that's a little different from the usual accuracy number you'd report on a test set. Standard evaluation asks: on the data distribution I happened to sample from, how often does the model get it right? Coverage asks a harder question, which is: for which inputs, for which subpopulations, for which regions of the input space, does the model actually have any business making a prediction at all?

And that framing matters for a couple of reasons. One is that aggregate accuracy can hide a lot. You can have ninety-five percent accuracy overall and be doing terribly on some group that makes up two percent of the data, and the average just won't show it. So part of coverage, for me, is asking how performance breaks down across many different slices, including slices you didn't necessarily anticipate when you built the model. That's where a lot of the fairness work I've done comes from, this idea that you want guarantees that hold not just for a handful of pre-specified protected groups, but for a rich, possibly combinatorial family of subgroups.

The other piece is more about epistemic humility on the model's part. There are inputs where the model should be saying, "I don't know," or "I haven't seen anything like this," and abstaining or deferring rather than confidently predicting. The learning-theory way to think about that is that your training data covers some region of the space, and outside of that region your generalization guarantees basically evaporate. So a well-behaved system should know where its coverage ends. Things like conformal prediction and selective classification are, in a sense, trying to make that boundary explicit, to say here's the set of inputs on which I'll commit to a prediction with a calibrated level of confidence, and here's where I won't.

And then the practical caveat, which I always want to add, is that coverage isn't free. If you demand good performance everywhere, on every subgroup, with honest abstention when you're uncertain, you're usually going to pay something in overall accuracy or in how often the model is willing to answer. So the interesting work isn't just measuring coverage, it's understanding those tradeoffs and deciding, often as a policy question rather than a technical one, which ones you're willing to make.

r001.rationale: The response discusses which inputs or subpopulations a model can predict on, but does not distinguish input coverage from output coverage.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention face recognition or natural variation in facial images.

astra-6.text:
I think about coverage as asking: Where have we actually measured how this model behaves? You can have a very large test set and a very accurate estimate of average performance, and still know very little about performance on particular populations or in particular circumstances.

If you’re evaluating a model for fairness, for example, you might look at error rates across a few demographic groups. That’s useful, but those averages can hide problems at the intersections of groups. A model might perform well on average for women, and well on average for older people, but poorly for older women.

So you want to examine a rich collection of subgroups. The challenge is that, as you make those groups more specific, you have fewer observations and more statistical uncertainty. Coverage isn’t simply checking more boxes; it’s understanding which claims your data can support, and where you still don’t have enough evidence.

r001.rationale: The response discusses coverage across populations and circumstances but does not distinguish input coverage from output coverage.

r002.rationale: The response gives a fairness subgroup example and does not mention face recognition or natural variation in facial images.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about coverage in terms of whose experience is actually represented in the evaluation. You can have a model that performs very well on average, but that average may conceal poor performance for a smaller population. So you want to ask: Which groups have we examined, and do we have enough data to say something meaningful about each of them?

And it’s not enough to check a few broad demographic categories. A model might look fine when you evaluate by race and fine when you evaluate by gender, but perform badly for a group defined by the intersection of those attributes. That pushes you toward examining a richer collection of subgroups, while being careful about statistical uncertainty. Coverage means looking broadly enough to discover those failures, and recognizing where your data doesn’t support a confident conclusion.
